items.claim: Jer.4.10’s disclosure calls itself complete but omits a rare-root catchword bracketing it with Jer.4.18, an undisclosed cross-seam cohesion signal.
items.evidence: The root נגע ("touch/reach") is rare — five verses in the whole book (sweep: 5 verses) — and two of the five are exactly the verses bracketing the false-peace complex: Jer.4.10 itself closes with “the sword reaches to the heart” (web:Jer.4.10), and Jer.4.18, eight verses later, closes with “it reaches to your heart” (web:Jer.4.18) — the same rare verb marking both ends of the intervening material. That is a byte-true catchword hook straddling this verse’s own back seam, left undisclosed even though the notes assert disclosure needs are already complete. The first-person address shift that opens Jer.4.10 remains a genuine internal seam on its own terms; the gap is the missing cross-seam disclosure, not the boundary itself.

items.claim: The impersonal future-passive opening at Jer.4.11 is a genuine, if softer, scene-shift seam correctly held at medium confidence, with both neighboring seams re-deriving cleanly and no petuchah/setumah mark misdisclosed.
items.evidence: Jer.4.11 opens “At that time it will be said…” (web:Jer.4.11), an impersonal forecast formula distinct in grammar and addressee-framing from Jer.4.10’s first-person direct address to Yahweh and from Jer.4.14’s imperative-plus-named-vocative opening (“Jerusalem, wash your heart…” web:Jer.4.14). No petuchah or setumah falls inside Jer.4.11-Jer.4.13 or at either boundary verse, matching the stated disclosure. The internal material, the wind/invader image running to the “Woe to us” (web:Jer.4.13) outcry, carries no imperative, vocative, or koh-amar restart of its own, so the span is not under-split against the granularity rule.

items.claim: The imperative-plus-vocative opening at Jer.4.14 and the embedded framing of the watchmen’s report both re-derive cleanly from the bytes, with the strongest merge rival explicitly named and rejected.
items.evidence: Jer.4.14 opens with a second-person imperative addressed by name, “Jerusalem, wash your heart from wickedness…” (web:Jer.4.14), distinct from Jer.4.11’s impersonal formula. The report introduced at Jer.4.15 (“For a voice declares from Dan…” web:Jer.4.15) carries its own imperatives at Jer.4.16, but these sit grammatically inside the reported voice’s own speech rather than opening a fresh address from the prophet to his audience, and the alternative of splitting Jer.4.15-Jer.4.17 into its own span is explicitly named and rejected on exactly that ground. The closing setumah at Jer.4.18 is disclosed and correctly held non-driving.

items.claim: The exclamatory first-person opening at Jer.4.19 is a well-marked seam, the doubled ketiv/qere at that verse and the internal setumah at Jer.4.21 are both correctly disclosed, and the voice-ambiguity at Jer.4.22 is honestly held open rather than silently decided.
items.evidence: Jer.4.19 opens with the exclamation “My anguish, my anguish!” (web:Jer.4.19), a clear return to first-person voice after the second-person address closing at Jer.4.18; the verse carries two ketiv/qere notes, correctly identified, with the cited splice drawn from before either note. The setumah at Jer.4.21, inside the span, and the one at Jer.4.18, at the front seam, are both disclosed and correctly held non-driving. At Jer.4.22 (“For my people are foolish. They don’t know me.” web:Jer.4.22) the possibility that a divine voice has displaced the prophet’s own is flagged rather than resolved, since no formal marker settles it either way — calibrated to the evidence rather than decided past it.
tier_citations: byte tier WEB quotation: web:Jer.4.19, web:Jer.4.22

items.claim: The four-fold ra’iti anaphora opening Jer.4.23-Jer.4.26 is byte-confirmed and the choice to hold the span outside the vision_report class is grounded in a real textual absence rather than merely asserted.
items.evidence: All four verses open with the same first-person seeing formula, “I saw” (web:Jer.4.23), a formal device absent from the surrounding lament and oracle material — a genuine four-fold anaphora repeated at web:Jer.4.24, web:Jer.4.25, and web:Jer.4.26. The comparison site named for holding this span outside the vision_report class, Jer.1.11-Jer.1.14, opens with a divine question-and-answer exchange, “Jeremiah, what do you see?” (web:Jer.1.11), that Jer.4.23-Jer.4.26 lacks; Jer.24.3 carries the same dialogue shape in its own wording. The closing setumah at Jer.4.26 is disclosed and held non-driving; the koh-amar onset at Jer.4.27 is a stronger marker than anything internal to this span, so the back seam is not under-cut.

items.claim: The alternative considered and rejected for Jer.4.27-Jer.4.31 is not demonstrably the strongest available rival: it never addresses the first-person perceptual shift at Jer.4.31.
items.evidence: Jer.4.31 opens with a כי-clause returning to first-person prophetic perception, “For I have heard a voice…” (web:Jer.4.31) — the same class of marker, an exclamatory or perceptual return to first-person voice, that elsewhere drives a fresh boundary: at Jer.4.10 (“Then I said…” web:Jer.4.10), at the opening cry of Jer.4.19, and again as the boundary separating Jer.5.3 from Jer.5.4 (“Then I said…” web:Jer.5.4). The alternative considered and rejected for this span addresses only Jer.4.29-Jer.4.30’s lack of an imperative, vocative, or koh-amar restart; it never names or rules out a cut at Jer.4.31 on this comparable ground. The koh-amar onset opening the unit at Jer.4.27 remains a strong, well-marked front seam; the gap is an unconsidered stronger rival for the unit’s internal cohesion, already held at medium confidence.

items.claim: The bare imperative opening Jer.5.1 is a strong, well-precedented seam type, and the chapter-crossing petuchah at Jer.4.31 is correctly disclosed as non-driving.
items.evidence: Jer.5.1 opens with a bare second-person-plural imperative, “Run back and forth through the streets of Jerusalem…” (web:Jer.5.1), the same discourse-imperative seam class used elsewhere in this stretch of the book; the span closes on the false-oath report of Jer.5.2 before Jer.5.3 turns to direct address of Yahweh. The petuchah at Jer.4.31, immediately before this span and across the chapter division, is disclosed and correctly held non-driving; the actual driver is the imperative, not the chapter number.

items.claim: The vocative address to Yahweh opening and closing Jer.5.3 is bracketed by two independently strong seams, and no disclosure gap survives inspection.
items.evidence: Jer.5.3 opens with direct vocative address, “O Yahweh, don’t your eyes look on truth?” (web:Jer.5.3), distinct from the imperative-addressed searchers of Jer.5.1-Jer.5.2, and Jer.5.4 reopens with emphatic first-person narration, “Then I said…” (web:Jer.5.4) — the same marker class this stretch elsewhere treats as boundary-driving. No petuchah, setumah, or ketiv/qere note falls at or adjacent to this verse, matching the claim that no further disclosure is needed.
